title: Islamic finance today
hook: banks, mortgages and sukuk, and debates about them

segments.voice: Yesterday, halal food today: the logo on the package, and tayyib, the word that asks for more. Your line was lawful and good. Which label did you read through? Today, from the plate to the wallet, and the end of a week. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-six.

A couple sits across a desk from a bank officer, holding a printout of a house they love. The numbers are fine. The officer slides over the paperwork, and one of them asks a question the officer may not hear every day: is there interest in this? Because if there is, for them, the house may be off the table. That question has built an entire corner of modern banking: Islamic finance, with its own mortgages, its own bonds, and its own arguments about whether it's done right.
screen: `A HOUSE THEY LOVE.` → `IS THERE INTEREST IN THIS?` → `A CORNER OF BANKING.`

segments.voice: The root is a line in Surah al-Baqarah. Some people said trade is just like usury, and the Qur'an answers, in Pickthall: "Allah permitteth trading and forbiddeth usury." The Arabic for usury is riba. And in Sahih Muslim, Jabir reports that the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, cursed the one who consumes riba, the one who pays it, the one who writes it down, and the two who witness it, and said they are all alike. So trade is open; earning money purely from lending money is not. How do you buy a house, then? Islamic banks offer a few shapes. In one, the bank buys the house and sells it to you at a known, fixed markup, paid over time. In another, the bank owns the house and you rent it, until it's yours. In a third, you and the bank buy it together as partners, and month by month you buy out the bank's share while paying rent on the part it still owns. Bonds have a version too: sukuk, certificates of part-ownership in a real asset, where the return comes from that asset rather than from a loan. And here's the debate, inside the tradition itself. Some scholars and critics say certain products are a conventional loan wearing an Arabic name: the monthly payment looks much the same. Others answer that the form is the substance: the bank really owns something, really carries risk, and that's a trade, not a loan. Muslims who care about this weigh both, and come down in different places.
screen: `ALLAH PERMITTETH TRADING.` · `THE BANK BUYS, THEN SELLS.` · `SUKUK: OWNING PART OF AN ASSET.` · `REAL TRADE, OR A NEW NAME?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn one product, starting with your own. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one money arrangement in your life: a credit card, a car payment, a rent, a loan to a friend, a savings account. Ask three quiet questions of it. Who owns what? Who carries the risk if things go wrong? Where does the extra money come from? You don't need to change anything. Just see it plainly. If you pray, you can hold your earnings in mind as something you'll be asked about. If you don't, simply hold the three questions. The bell holds the time.
Islamic finance today. Banks, mortgages and sukuk built around one verse: trade is permitted, riba is forbidden, and the arguments over where one ends and the other begins. Today's word.

Your line: finance without interest. Today, look up one Islamic finance product and ask who owns what. And look back at this week: minorities, science, the body, the earth, the mosque, the plate, and now the wallet. Tomorrow, rejecting extremism. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: Muslims who avoid interest may use home financing from Islamic banks built on sale, lease or partnership, invest in sukuk, and consult scholars or Sharia boards on products, while some decide certain products are too close to conventional loans.

fork.setup: you want a home, and you won't pay interest. an Islamic bank offers to buy the house with you as partners. what happens next?
options: you pay interest on the bank's half.
you buy out the bank's share over time, paying rent on what it still owns.

fork.reveal: in the partnership model, you buy the bank's share bit by bit, and pay rent on the part it still owns. critics say the payment can look much like a mortgage; defenders say real ownership changes it.

trapdoor: what you thought: Islamic finance means no profit.
what it means: trade and profit are permitted; riba, money earned purely from lending money, is not. banks use sale, lease and partnership instead.
what a scholar hears: 2:275 and the curse in Sahih Muslim on all parties to riba, then a live debate on whether some products differ from loans in substance or only in form.
